claims.statement: The CISA/Siemens advisory (ICSA-22-286-15) documents a cross-site scripting vulnerability in affected SCALANCE products and states that, if used by a threat actor, it could result in session cookie theft and session hijacking.
The CISA/Siemens advisory recommends product updates to the latest versions and protection of network access to the affected devices as mitigation measures for the described session-hijacking risk.

The CISA/Siemens advisory uses conditional language ('if used by a threat actor could result in') when describing session cookie theft and session hijacking as a possible consequence of exploiting the identified cross-site scripting vulnerability in a specific product family.

The IBM X-Force 2024 excerpt reports security misconfigurations as the most observed OWASP web application risk globally in 2024 penetration-testing findings and identifies concurrent user sessions as a top misconfiguration offense that could weaken MFA through session hijacking.

The IBM X-Force 2024 excerpt ties session hijacking to 2024 penetration-testing observations about misconfigurations, reporting concurrent user sessions at 15% and excessive session timeouts at 8% within the misconfiguration category.

NIST SP 800-53 Rev.5 describes session authenticity protection as addressing man-in-the-middle attacks, session hijacking, and insertion of false information, and includes a control enhancement to invalidate session identifiers at logout.

The supplied Crossref cutoff-constrained trend for the PMT_HTTPS query reports annual publication counts of 14 in 2021, 8 in 2022, 8 in 2023, and 15 in 2024, with a positive OLS slope of 0.300000 works/year, first-to-last delta of 1, and total_results of 45; the record explicitly states it is an external publication-activity validation axis independent of the Scopus-derived NoP model input and does not establish deployment maturity, operational effectiveness, or causal mitigation effectiveness.

The supplied individual Crossref records are publication-metadata records for specific DOIs, including a physics scattering paper (10.32014/2019.2518-1726.30), a Spideroak/Whisper Systems/Silent Circle record (10.1080/07317131.2015.1000731), and a Liver King record (10.1111/rsr.16328); they do not provide directional PMT or threat trajectory evidence.

The supplied MITRE ATT&CK records describe BOOTRASH as a bootkit targeting Windows operating systems used by threat actors targeting the financial sector, and ASPXSpy as a web shell modified by Threat Group-3390; these are adversary-software context records that do not establish session-hijacking NoI/NoP trajectory or gap direction.
